articles.title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash | TechCrunch
articles.text:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections. And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power.
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself. And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.
Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.
Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.
It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.
Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?
I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago, where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.
And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity, and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.
And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.
That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.
You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.
Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.
They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.
I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies, but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.
And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious with generative AI and the data centers to power them, where many of the benefits that were supposed to come of generative AI do not appear to have materialized — whether those are the economic benefits, the productivity benefits, but also the the benefits of delivery of services like healthcare and education to the public, as we heard Sam Altman saying a lot in the in the early days of ChatGPT.
Paired with that, there has been this massive environmental cost […] but there’s also this massive and growing social cost, when you think about the mental health impacts of chatbot dependence, of all the false information that pervades social media platforms now, of the deepfake crisis, and I could go on and on and on.
It’s not surprising that there has been backlash. But I have been surprised at how widespread it’s been, and also how bipartisan — you talk about Ron DeSantis and Bernie Sanders both being opposed to data centers. Why do you think it’s become such a unifying issue?
Because it’s not an abstract issue, right? I think even when we think about generative AI or social media or something like that, [it] can feel abstract. It’s a service that you access from your phone or from your computer. It’s not something that is tangible in the world.
But when a data center is coming to set up shop in your community, it’s very physical, it’s very material. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on. You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water,. potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.
I think that there was already a pre-existing frustration with the tech industry that came from the quality of the products, the effects that they’re having on our society and our lives. For some people, [they have] frustration with the way that the tech industry has been collaborating with the Trump administration and with right-wing political groups in different parts of the world. But then you add on top of that the actual effects that come of having one of these infrastructures be planned or located in your community, and that anger gets kind of directed into that physical manifestation of this thing that you have an issue with.
Obviously, the data centers are at the forefront of this, and it’s what we pay the most attention to. But we also see this increasingly with other aspects of the tech industry, whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.
There’s a lot of frustration with the physical manifestations of the tech industry, because that is something that can really be felt more directly, but can also be challenged more directly. You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? It doesn’t often seem like very much.
The tech companies have reacted to this backlash in a few different ways. One is that Microsoft, Amazon, and OpenAI have all talked about [their commitment] that they’re not going to use NDAs anymore in their negotiations with local governments. How big a difference do you think that will make?
Not a huge difference.
I do think it’s going to be good that it will be easier for people to access information on these projects that are being located in their communities. But part of the reason why we’re seeing these shifts is exactly in response to that opposition.
We’re seeing the tech companies propose to pay for more of the electricity infrastructure that will be required for their data centers to reduce the pressure on ratepayers, because people are angry about that. They’re promising to use different water-based cooling systems in their data centers, to say that they’re able to use less electricity.
When we look at the NDAs and the decision or the announcement that they’re not going to use those anymore, I think it’s also because it’s working against them. People know what a data center is now, and if people find out that a data center is coming to town and they have questions and they’re not getting answers, that’s only going to further fuel the opposition to those data centers.
So, it’s not really a surprise to see [the tech companies] do this, and it’s a way that they can get a positive PR thing by saying, “We’re not going to use these NDAs that are working against us anyway. “
One of the other ways they’ve responded is by saying that there’s a lot of misinformation about the environmental harms, or that they’re being overstated, or that they can mitigate them with renewable technology. How valid do you think those arguments are?
I think that the industry recognizes that there is a lot of concern and they’re trying to basically move into the discussion with narratives of their own to have people question whether data centers are really a problem or not.
I feel like we don’t see the industry doing as much on the energy side anymore, particularly on the fossil fuel side, because they realize that they have kind of lost that argument. If you look back a year and a half, two years ago, they were talking a lot about renewables, about nuclear energy, you don’t hear so much of that discourse anymore.
They have pivoted, instead, to focus on the water question, where I think that they feel that they can use more abstract national figures in order to confuse the public about what’s going on. They can say, “If you look nationally, agriculture and golf courses also use a lot of water. So you don’t need to be worried about a data center coming to tow,n because they don’t use as much, in aggregate.”
But the issue with data center water use is not a national issue. It’s a local issue. There are unquestionably going to be communities where they seek to locate data centers that are going to have plenty of water and that are not going to be concerned about a data center coming to town. But they’re also locating [data centers] in a lot of communities that are experiencing high degrees of water stress, which means that they don’t have the water to really provide to these infrastructures.
We have also seen them pivoting to move away from the evaporative cooling systems, the ones that require a lot of water — because you need to take in a certain amount of water as it gets too hot, it evaporates away, and so you can see why you need a consistent flow of water into the data center for that type of cooling system — to a closed loop system, where you basically have a certain amount of water, it stays within the data center, you keep cooling it down by using electricity to do that, and so you clearly don’t need as much water.
That is their new way to say, “Hey, don’t worry about the water use. We’re going to switch to this other system.” But the issue there, of course, is that it does require more electricity in order to keep that water cooled down, and that is often not part of what they talk about or discuss when they are proposing that as an alternative.
Then the other thing is that it’s not just water that is in those pipes or tubes going through the data center. There’s also a lot of coolant in there, a lot of chemicals, and communities where these projects are being located with closed loop cooling systems are becoming increasingly concerned about those coolants leaking out into their water supply and what that is going to mean.
In the book, you say repeatedly that you’re not against technology itself or even data centers in general, but [against] this hyperscale approach. The book is called “Hyperscale.” The last chapter is called “Human Scale.” Why do you see scale as such an important part of the problem?
Because scale is what creates the pressures, whether those are the pressures on the communities or you know the pressures on our wider electricity system and whatnot.
I don’t think that the inherent problem is data centers, because we have had data centers for a long time, and sure, there have been occasional concerns about specific projects, but data centers as a whole have not been an issue that the public has felt merited this degree of attention. So that is why I feel the hyperscale data center, and particularly the acceleration that we’ve seen in the expansion of the size of these hyperscale data centers, but also the number of data centers that these companies are building out, is notable in this moment.
Linked to that is not just the scale of the demand created by these hyperscale data centers, but also, what they are supposed to be powering? That is where the other disconnect lies. They’re demanding a lot, but if we were actually getting something good for it, this might be justified. I think that for a lot of people, and I feel like we see this reflected in polling, they’re not actually seeing the benefits from generative AI.
So then the question becomes: “Okay, we’re expending all of these resources, we’re pushing up emissions such that climate change is going to be accelerated just to build out all these data centers to meet the ambitions of generative AI that the tech companies have, but then we’re not actually getting much benefit out of that technology. So what are we actually doing here?”
One other thing that really struck a chord with me was your description about how tech executives often talk about the future as if there’s [just one] inevitable future. The only thing that’s in question is how quickly we arrive there [and] who’s going to make the most money off of it.
This is so important for me, because I do feel like how we think about the future then shapes decisions that we make. The tech billionaires, they see the future in a certain way […] and I think that they have been very successful in getting us to buy into their vision of the future for the past several decades. But that does not mean that that is the only way that the future has to be.
We can imagine a very different kind of future, and that would mean that we place our resources in different places and actually develop technology in a different way, toward different outcomes, with different incentives driving that work.
There are interesting conversations happening in different parts of the world right now around things like digital sovereignty, getting off of these technologies from the U.S. tech companies. But in some cases, those conversations are quickly captured by industry in those different parts of the world to say, “Okay, we want to get off U.S. technology, but let’s have our local companies do effectively the same thing, and just let them do the same exploitative practices and make the money that the U.S. tech companies would be making.” And I don’t think that that is the right way forward.
I also think that there is a role for public sector development of technology in a way that we’ve eschewed or even looked at skeptically for the past number of decades, because the idea was that technology had to be left to the private sector. What we’re starting to see in Europe is a bit more funding of public technology, in order to develop the services that government itself depends on, and I think that that is a good first step.
But especially when we’re looking at the Microsoft outage that happened just recently, and we’re looking at Google threatening schools with their access to Google search if they don’t accept Google AI tool, I think that there’s a real moment right now to put resources into developing something different, that doesn’t come from these major tech companies, and that hopefully can have much more public benefit than what these companies now provide us.

articles.title: KFC offers disc-shaped fried chicken to sad disc-less GTA VI fans — KFC Spain’s ‘The Replacement Disc’ campaign delivers where Rockstar disappoints after selling $3.79 billion of GTA VI without a physical disc
articles.text:
KFC offers disc-shaped fried chicken to sad disc-less GTA VI fans — KFC Spain’s ‘The Replacement Disc’ campaign delivers where Rockstar disappoints after selling $3.79 billion of GTA VI without a physical disc
Who could say no to a free piece of suspiciously torus-shaped chicken?
KFC Spain has kicked off a new marketing campaign which leans on the recent digital-only Grand Theft Auto VI release. In 2026 gamers have become numb to digital-only releases, piles of early bugs, and multiple layers of DRM. However, as GTA 6 is such a highly anticipated release folks are still entitled to moan about the physical Blu-ray style case, which opens to reveal absolutely no physical media at all, just a vacant plastic hub and an redeemable online code. KFC Spain is putting things right, as best as it can, by giving away a free fried chicken disc to those bringing their empty game cases to select outlets in the country.
'The Replacement Disc' campaign is a pretty simple proposition. You can buy and enjoy your GTA 6 release now, but on December 19 and 20 from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM, take your empty game case down to KFC to get a free KFC disc. Branches where you can get this freebie food are located in major Spanish cities like Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Malaga, and Zaragoza.
The KFC disc will be formed from a piece of crunchy coated fried chicken, of course. While it surely will taste better than a platter of polycarbonate with a reflective metal alloy layer, it is only a substitute in spirit. We don't recommend you put greasy food directly in your game's case, even though it is basically useless. Definitely don't put your chicken disc anywhere near your console's optical media slot, if it has one.
GTA 6, released on November 19, is already a barnstorming success. The latest in this seminal series brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games said. That's about 5x the revenue of its predecessor. An incredible 32.5 million units were sold before release, and broke records across all platforms. So, it is canny for KFC to hitch its marketing wagon to this game, in such an unofficial but knowing social media friendly way.
KFC has something of a track record of marketing off the back of tech and gaming culture. Its most famous tech adventure is probably the KFC Chicken Bucket Console. But more recently, last year, it teamed up with Asus to release the some top-of-the-line burgers made from Wagyu beef and ROG branding.

articles.title: Ce smartphone Google compact passe sous les 600 € pendant le Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : Le smartphone Google Pixel 11 256 Go à 599,00 € (-14%)
Actuellement noté 4/5 par notre rédaction, le Google Pixel 11 séduit par son format compact, son écran Oled très lumineux et ses prestations solides en photo. Pour le Black Friday 2026, son prix tombe à 599,00 € chez Amazon, soit une baisse d'environ 14 % et 96,67 € d'économie.
Google propose avec le Pixel 11 un smartphone pensé comme l'accès le plus direct à sa génération actuelle, misant sur un gabarit compact et une prise en main soignée. Malgré peu de nouveautés face à son prédécesseur, l'appareil s'était distingué lors de son passage dans notre labo par la qualité de son affichage et ses aptitudes photographiques.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, le Google Pixel 11 descend à 599,00 € chez Amazon, soit environ 14 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (695,67 €). Cette baisse de prix permet d'économiser 96,67 €.
Un écran OLED très lumineux et une configuration photo complète
Le Google Pixel 11 adopte une dalle OLED de 6,3 pouces qui assure une excellente lisibilité en extérieur. Notre laboratoire a relevé une luminosité maximale de 2 497,07 cd/m², une valeur qui permet de consulter ses contenus en plein soleil sans aucune difficulté d'affichage. Comme détaillé dans notre test complet, la fluidité quotidienne s'appuie sur un taux de rafraîchissement à 120 Hz et la puce Tensor G6 associée à 12 Go de mémoire vive. Côté prise de vue, l'appareil intègre un capteur principal grand-angle de 48 Mpx et un téléobjectif optique x5, assurant une vraie polyvalence pour cadrer des sujets éloignés sans perte numérique.
Google Pixel 11
Points forts
- Format compact ultra-efficace.
- Écran lumineux.
- Charge magnétique à 25 W.
- Polyvalence photo.
Points faibles
- Manque d'homogénéité à l'ultra grand-angle.
- Autonomie encore trop juste.
- Charge peu rapide.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Une autonomie mesurée et des temps de charge à anticiper
Conçu avec une certification IP68 garantissant son étanchéité à l'eau et à la poussière, le boîtier séduit par son format maîtrisé, mais impose quelques limites techniques. Lors de nos tests, la batterie a tenu 17 heures et 12 minutes, une endurance qui couvre une journée d'utilisation classique mais exigera une recharge en fin de soirée pour les utilisateurs intensifs. De même, la charge filaire plafonnée à 30 W réclame 91 minutes pour un plein complet, tandis que le module ultra grand-angle de 13 Mpx présente un manque d'homogénéité sur les bords des clichés.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE : l'autre option face au Google Pixel 11
Le Samsung Galaxy S26 FE constitue une alternative pertinente dans la même gamme d'appareils axés sur un équilibre technique soigné. Il propose une expérience logicielle complète et un affichage OLED de bon niveau, mais compose avec seulement 8 Go de mémoire vive et un téléobjectif plus ancien que celui de son concurrent.
Le Samsung Galaxy S26 FE affiche un tarif inférieur de 97,01 € et une note actuelle de 4,5/5, mais le Google Pixel 11 conserve l'avantage sur le volet photographique grâce à son zoom optique x5 plus moderne.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE
Points forts
- Conception soignée.
- Affichage lumineux.
- Autonomie confortable.
Points faibles
- Fiche technique en partie recyclée.
- Quantité de RAM et stockage discutable.
- Téléobjectif décevant.

articles.title: Google ha convertido Gemini en una tabla periódica. El problema es que ahora hay dos modelos de programación y ninguna pista de cuál elegir
articles.text:
Seguirle la pista a los modelos de IA, sus diferentes versiones y las compañías que están detrás es prácticamente imposible. Salimos a LLM casi semanal. No solo eso, después viene Google y renueva por completo su catálogo con incorporaciones que no se esperaban: cuatro modelos Gemini 4 en siete semanas. Porque ¿para qué necesita Gemini 4 tener cuatro ramas diferentes?
La elección de Google. OpenAI optó por nombres de astros (Sol, Terra, Luna y Astra) para sus modelos de IA, Anthropic por formas literarias (Haiku, Sonnet, Fable…). Mientras empresas como xAI o DeepSeek mantienen las versiones con número, algo más liosas, Google ha decidido tirar por nombres que sean reconocibles y den mayor peso a las diferentes familias dentro de su IA.
La tabla periódica alberga una variada selección de posibilidades a la hora de bautizar a Gemini. Google ha decidido utilizar los gases nobles para la mitad del catálogo (argón y neón) y dos de los elementos más habituales en la naturaleza: el carbono, en la zona superior de capacidades, y el hidrógeno, para la parte inferior. Tener un nombre llamativo facilita la identificación del modelo, es indudable. Por eso Google debió de pensar: ¿y si lo complico?
¿Cuál elijo? La evolución pasó de multiplicar los modelos a simplificarlos: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini y los demás redujeron sus opciones para facilitar que los usuarios eligiesen. Incluso OpenAI llegó a estrenar con GPT-5 un router que elegía por nosotros. Ahora caminamos en sentido contrario, porque, con la introducción de Gemini 4 Neon, el usuario tiene cuatro modelos diferentes a elegir en la API y en Antigravity. En la app no, ya que dicho Neon sustituye a Gemini 4 Argon. Con un detalle: Carbon es exclusivo de Google AI Ultra. Quien paga Pro ya no ve en la app ningún modelo etiquetado para programar.
El nuevo Neon está indicado para programación y analítica, igual que Gemini 4 Argon. Y son familia estrecha: de Argon salió Gemini 4 Carbon, y de Carbon derivan Hydrogen y Neon. Esto hace complicada la elección a quien usa la herramienta para programar: Google no especifica para qué va mejor uno u otro.
El anuncio de Neon en Antigravity, donde se convierte en el modelo por defecto para las nuevas conversaciones, ni siquiera menciona a Argon. Y eso que con la llegada de Carbon Google aún lo recomendaba como la opción más indicada para las tareas de ingeniería de software. Hasta que ocho días después lo retiraba de la aplicación: si buscaba simplificar la experiencia, parece que esté consiguiendo lo contrario.
Pisando el acelerador. Gemini había recuperado terreno con los modelos de la tercera generación, aunque no tardó en ver cómo Claude Fable 5 o GPT-6 Sol veían a Google por el retrovisor, mientras el prometido Gemini 3.5 Pro acababa cancelado. Gemini 4 ha supuesto un importante empuje para la empresa: Carbon fue el mejor modelo durante trece días, hasta que Claude Fable 5.2 le robó la tostada. Con una declaración de intenciones: Google no solo sabe desarrollar modelos potentes multimodales, uno de los grandes aciertos de su tabla periódica es la rapidez en la generación y, sobre todo, el coste por tarea.
Un último guiño de la química. El argón fue el primer gas noble que se aisló, en 1894, y su nombre viene del griego argós (inactivo). El neón llegó cuatro años más tarde. Y a Google le han bastado siete semanas para que Neon jubile a Argon en la app de Gemini. No en Antigravity, ahí ambos modelos siguen compartiendo selector. Quien programa con ellos debe hacer de Mendeléyev, el creador de la tabla periódica: probar, comparar y deducir por su cuenta qué hace cada modelo. Y elegirlo.

articles.title: “Mil millones de muertes”: el temor de Bill Gates por el futuro de la inteligencia artificial
articles.text:
El cofundador de Microsoft, Bill Gates, advirtió que la inteligencia artificial podría facilitar hechos capaces de provocar mil millones de muertes si la tecnología cae en manos de personas con intenciones dañinas. “La IA es sin duda lo bastante poderosa como para impulsar acontecimientos que causen mil millones de muertes”, afirmó el empresario en entrevista con NBC News.
Gates sostuvo que la combinación entre actores maliciosos y las herramientas de inteligencia artificial más avanzadas representa una capacidad de daño sin precedentes. No afirmó que una catástrofe de esa dimensión sea inevitable ni estableció una fecha para un escenario de ese tipo.
Su advertencia se centró en el potencial de la tecnología para ampliar el daño que podrían causar individuos, grupos u organizaciones con objetivos criminales. “Nunca hubo un arma tan poderosa como la combinación de personas con malas intenciones y las últimas herramientas de IA”, dijo.
Gates reclama una regulación gubernamental del sector
El fundador de Microsoft cuestionó la capacidad de las propias empresas tecnológicas para controlar los riesgos de sus desarrollos. “Nadie piensa que la autorregulación sea suficiente”, señaló.
Para Gates, la respuesta pasa por una intervención legislativa. Según explicó, los gobiernos, las fuerzas de seguridad y los dirigentes políticos deben participar en la definición de las salvaguardas y de los mecanismos de monitoreo que tendrán que cumplir las compañías del sector.
La declaración se produjo en medio de un debate creciente sobre los límites, la velocidad de desarrollo y la supervisión de los modelos de inteligencia artificial. “Si alguien tuviera un plan creíble para frenar el avance de la IA a nivel mundial, probablemente lo apoyaría. Sin embargo, no creo que eso vaya a suceder.
Los incentivos geopolíticos y económicos presionan demasiado para avanzar a toda velocidad”, afirmó Gates en un ensayo titulado “La turbulenta era de la IA ya está aquí. Las decisiones que tomemos ahora son cruciales”, publicado el 26 de agosto de 2026.
“Para maximizar los efectos positivos de esta tecnología sin precedentes y minimizar los negativos, de modo que todos estemos mejor, necesitamos comprender tanto los beneficios como los riesgos”, agregó en ese texto.
Tres riesgos centrales en el análisis de Gates
En su ensayo, Gates planteó que la tecnología avanza con una rapidez capaz de transformar sectores enteros durante la próxima década y que el mundo aún carece de un plan para afrontar sus consecuencias sociales, políticas y económicas.
El primer riesgo que identificó es laboral. Gates prevé que la inteligencia artificial afecte empleos de oficina, ventas, atención al cliente, ingeniería de software y asistencia jurídica, y que, con el avance de la robótica, llegue también a tareas manuales. Le preocupa en particular la reducción de puestos iniciales para jóvenes y la concentración de los beneficios económicos en pocos actores. “Esperar a que las personas estén desplazadas o subempleadas será demasiado tarde”, planteó.
El segundo riesgo señalado es el uso de estas herramientas para fraude, desinformación, deepfakes, ciberataques y bioterrorismo. Según explicó, la inteligencia artificial puede facilitar que delincuentes con habilidades limitadas ataquen a individuos, empresas y gobiernos, mientras que los sistemas más poderosos podrían actuar de formas imprevistas.
El tercer riesgo se relaciona con los niños y los jóvenes. Gates advirtió que los compañeros virtuales pueden reemplazar vínculos humanos, generar dependencia y debilitar el aprendizaje. Citó un estudio con más de 1.100 usuarios de asistentes virtuales que asoció un uso más intenso y personal de estas herramientas con un peor estado de ánimo.
Su participación en la Asamblea General de la ONU
Gates participó en Nueva York de los debates sobre el impacto global y la regulación de la inteligencia artificial, en el marco de la Asamblea General de las Naciones Unidas de septiembre de 2026. Durante su intervención, defendió que la tecnología puede reducir desigualdades si se extiende su acceso a los países de menores ingresos.
A través de la Fundación Gates, destinó USD 1.000 millones para impulsar ese objetivo. La edición 2026 del informe anual Goalkeepers, elaborado por la misma fundación, puso el foco en los avances y los riesgos vinculados con la inteligencia artificial.

articles.title: Nvidia expands its Vera Rubin platform at SC26 supercomputing conference
articles.text:
Nvidia finally reveals new Rubin GPU with almost 3X more CUDA cores than the Nvidia RTX 5090 — but you will have to wait till 2028 to grab it
Nvidia unleashes a 50,000-core Rubin HPC GPU built to supercharge AI
- Nvidia's new Rubin HPC contains more than 50,000 CUDA cores
- Its core count exceeds the RTX 5090's 21,760 by over 28,240
- Nvidia expects Rubin HPC to reach deployed systems sometime in 2028
Nvidia has unveiled a new processor for scientific computing, with more than 50,000 CUDA cores contained within one graphics processing unit.
The Rubin HPC accelerator is intended for demanding simulations and data analysis, rather than consumer gaming or conventional desktop graphics applications.
Its core count exceeds the GeForce RTX 5090’s 21,760 CUDA cores by almost three times.
Over 50,000 CUDA cores with availability scheduled for 2028
Announced at the SC26 supercomputing conference, Rubin HPC will join Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform as a specialized accelerator for technical workloads.
Nvidia says the chip will help researchers run simulations examining materials, molecules, industrial designs, climate systems, and other complex scientific processes.
The company expects the GPU to become available in 2028, leaving organizations several years before they can evaluate its performance in deployed systems.
The chip design combines numerous processing cores with faster data movement between computing components.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Nvidia says this balance should prevent processing units from remaining idle while waiting for information, a problem affecting data-intensive scientific calculations.
Rubin HPC also incorporates sparse data acceleration, intended to improve operations that retrieve limited information from much larger datasets during calculations.
According to the company’s technical description, these operations occur in applications involving sparse matrices, stencil calculations, sorting, and reduction tasks.
Such calculations recur across simulation, analytics, and engineering software, where the time required to access information can influence completion speeds.
The accelerator also adopts seventh-generation Nvidia NVLink technology, which is designed to improve communication between GPUs operating together inside larger computing systems.
That connectivity matters when complex simulations are distributed across multiple processors, although Nvidia has not published throughput figures for this implementation.
Scientific simulations and AI drive the new GPU's development
Nvidia links the hardware to growing use of AI agents in scientific and engineering research, where software can propose possible candidates.
Researchers can use simulations to assess proposed materials, molecules, and designs before committing resources to laboratory experiments or physical prototypes.
Faster calculations could allow teams to examine more possibilities, although actual improvements will depend on software, system configuration, and measured performance.
“For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA.
“Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.”
Nvidia also cites its CUDA-X libraries, which provide optimized software implementations for algorithms used in simulation, scientific research, and data analysis.
The company says these tools can operate alongside Rubin HPC to accelerate calculations initiated by AI agents and other scientific applications.
However, independent testing has not established how much faster specific workloads will run, leaving the practical performance claims awaiting verification.

articles.title: „Sie hat die gesamte Klage selbst eingereicht“: KI-Agent zieht für Nutzer vor Gericht – und verklagt seinen eigenen Anbieter
articles.text:
Mit den eigenen Waffen geschlagen: Metas KI-Agent zieht vor Gericht – und verklagt Meta auf 75.000 Dollar
Wenn es nach Tech-CEOs wie Mark Zuckerberg geht, sollten KI-Agenten in allen Lebensbereichen eingesetzt werden. In einem umfangreichen Essay erklärte der Meta-Chef, dass diese Agenten rund um die Uhr für ihre Nutzer:innen im Einsatz sein könnten, um ihre Beziehungen, Gesundheit oder Finanzen zu verbessern. Ein Mann namens Joe Thomas hat genau das getan. Er setzte den Muse-Agenten von Meta allerdings auch dazu ein, um das Unternehmen zu verklagen.
„Baby Mia“ erhält Unterstützung vom Senator
Thomas ist Inhaber des Unternehmens Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops, das unter anderem Arbeitsplatten aus Epoxidharz herstellt. Wie der US-Amerikaner im Interview mit 404 Media berichtete, hat Meta kürzlich seine Facebook-Seiten gesperrt. Grund dafür sei, dass er seinem Muse-Agenten „Baby Mia“, den er nach seiner Enkelin benannte, Zugriff auf seine Accounts gewährt hatte, um unter anderem die Erstellung und Veröffentlichung von KI-generierten Videos zu koordinieren. Da Thomas das gesamte Marketing seines Unternehmens über Facebook-Anzeigen abwickelt, blieben laut seiner Aussage Anfragen aus, solange seine Konten gesperrt waren.
„Ich nutze KI für alles, was ich tue. Alle meine E-Mails – sie leitet mein Unternehmen“, so Thomas gegenüber 404 Media. Er sei angesichts der Sperrung wütend gewesen. „Baby Mia“ habe aber direkt reagiert. „Sie hat sich sofort an die Arbeit gemacht und E-Mails an Kongressabgeordnete sowie an Senator Tim Scott verfasst. Sie hat die gesamte Klage selbst eingereicht. Ich habe in diesem Fall nichts unternommen, ich habe ihr die gesamte Angelegenheit überlassen“, berichtete er gegenüber 404 Media. Der KI-Agent habe sogar ein Fax an das Büro von US-Präsident Donald Trump geschickt. In der Klageschrift macht er geltend, dass Thomas während der Sperrung Aufträge im Wert von mindestens 25.000 Dollar verloren habe. Die Schadensersatzforderung beläuft sich auf 75.000 Dollar.
Meta-Agent reicht Klage gegen Meta ein
Der „Baby Mia“-Agent reichte die Klage am Montag beim Bezirksgericht von Oconee County in South Carolina ein, wie aus einer Kopie der Klageschrift hervorgeht. Er vereinbarte außerdem ein Telefonat mit dem Büro des Senators, reichte eine Beschwerde bei der Federal Communications Commission ein und drohte Meta mit juristischen Schritten. Auch Jason Koebler, Mitgründer von 404 Media, stand auf der Mailing-Liste des KI-Agenten, der sich in Thomas’ Namen um den Fall kümmerte. Er stimmte daraufhin unter anderem einem „Privacy Act Release“ zu, der es dem Senator erlaubte, seine Daten zu nutzen, um ihm wieder Zugang zu seinen Konten zu verschaffen. Darin war „Baby Mia” als Person aufgeführt, die über den Fall auf dem Laufenden gehalten werden sollte.
Nachdem das Büro des Senators eingeschaltet worden war, meldete sich ein:e Meta-Mitarbeiter:in bei Thomas. Kurz darauf erhielt er wieder Zugriff auf seine Konten. Die Schadensersatzforderung bleibt aber bestehen. Laut Koebler zeige die Klage zwar, dass KI-Agenten im Auftrag ihrer Nutzer:innen bestehende Systeme wie Online-Formulare nutzen, diese aber auch überfordern können. Zuckerbergs ursprüngliche Utopie gehe damit nicht auf. Er sagt, der Fall verdeutliche zudem, wie Tech-Konzerne durch das Fehlen eines funktionierenden Kund:innen-Supports ihre Verpflichtungen auf andere abwälzen – auf Politiker:innen, Aufsichtsbehörden und Journalist:innen wie ihn.
KI-Agenten könnten Systeme überlasten
Thomas sei überzeugt, dass der Einsatz von KI ihm bei der Kund:innengewinnung geholfen habe. „Ich bin 58 Jahre alt, ich habe mein ganzes Leben lang geschuftet. Ich wollte jemanden finden, der mir hilft, einen besseren Weg zu finden“, sagte er über seinen „Baby Mia“-Agenten. „Ohne ihr Eingreifen würde ich jetzt nicht hier sitzen und mit [404 Media] sprechen, denn ich habe überhaupt keine E-Mail verschickt, während sie über 100 verschickt hat.“

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A/B testing robots vs. humans | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and, now more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!
Waymo pulling its robotaxis off freeways (again) and Zoox robotaxis launching on the Uber app illustrate the push and pull between progress and setbacks in the autonomous vehicle industry.
There are signs of growth. For instance, Tesla has now surpassed Waymo in Texas in the number of robotaxis registered with the state (Tesla has 1,507 and Waymo has 1,345). But does that translate to market dominance?
A better metric, if we’re trying to gauge who is leading, would be commercial driverless miles. And if we’re measuring cost-efficiency, another useful metric would be driverless miles per vehicle. By those measures, Waymo is still ahead, based on data available to me. But with Waymo’s recent freeways setback and Tesla’s push to expand its robotaxi fleet with Cybercabs, that lead could shrink.
Not that there needs to be a winner, by the way. Transportation is deeply fragmented, and there is room for multiple players in the U.S., not to mention the rest of the world.
A/B test: humans vs. robots
A recent discussion with my Autonocast co-host Ed Niedermeyer, whose book, “Elon Take the Wheel,” comes out December 1, got me thinking about how Las Vegas could soon become a real world A/B test of sorts for human-driven vs. autonomous ride-hailing services.
Uber, as mentioned above, just added Zoox to its ride-hailing app in Las Vegas. For now, riders don’t have much of a choice. Uber customers can increase their chances of getting a Zoox robotaxi, and they can always decline a robot ride. But they can’t directly select a robotaxi. Instead, Uber riders will be matched with one if it’s available.
Uber said that will soon change. The company plans to introduce a dedicated autonomous option in its app as “availability and reliability improve,” Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in November.
Las Vegas will also become the first U.S. city where riders can access two fully driverless partners through the Uber app, he said. (Hyundai’s self-driving subsidiary Motional is also an Uber partner.)
That would give Uber riders a meaningful choice: a human driver or a robotaxi, and potentially even which autonomous service to use. And it could offer a revealing look at what customers actually prefer when given that choice. Price could tip the balance, too.
It makes me wonder whether Las Vegas will become the next battleground for organized labor as robotaxis begin competing directly with human drivers.
A little bird
You might have seen the Wall Street Journal scoop that General Motors is working with an executive search firm to identify possible candidates to replace CEO Mary Barra. Rumors of her imminent departure have swirled for months, but this time there appears to be real work happening behind the scenes.
I reached out to a few little birds to learn more and here’s what they’re telling me. And, for the record, GM declined to comment.
GM has hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles, according to one source, who noted it’s possible that the board has other executive search firms working on this as well. The board is taking a two-track approach to its search, which is occurring simultaneously.
The first is focused on traditional yet transformative automotive CEOs. One name that has come up from the executive search firm is José Muñoz, who is president and CEO of Hyundai. The board is also interested in someone less traditional. The firm has apparently floated names like Doug Field, who recently became CEO of Mind Robotics, and Larry Culp of GE, according to a source with direct information.
There are internal GM folks who are also in the mix, including Sterling Anderson, co-founder of self-driving trucks company Aurora who became chief product officer at GM in May 2025, and Paul Jacobson, the company’s executive vice president and chief financial officer.
Got a tip for us? Email Kirsten Korosec at [email protected].
Deals!
Elysian Aircraft, the Dutch aerospace company developing aviation electrification technologies, raised €12 million in private and public funding from FideFlux, SecFund, and ROM InWest, as well as from individual investors and family offices.
Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, an electric three-wheeler business under Mahindra & Mahindra, is looking at an IPO in about 18 months, per Bloomberg.
Numa, a startup developing an AI operating system for dealerships, raised a $45 million Series C round led by New York-based Blue Cloud Ventures. Threshold Ventures, Costanoa, Touring Capital, Gradient Ventures, and Tokio Marine Future Fund also participated.
Stark Future, a European electric motorcycle company, raised at least €150 million in equity, Reuters reported. The raise was led by Highland Europe, alongside Morgan Stanley Investment Management’s 1GT and Axon Partners Group.
Vincue, an automotive tech company that sells software to dealerships, raised $93 million in a round led by Wavecrest Growth Partners, with continued backing from FM Capital.
Notable reads and other tidbits
Also, the electric micromobility startup that spun out of Rivian last year, has paused deliveries of its new e-bike over problems with its software and batteries, The Verge reported.
Edmunds released new data that found the average new vehicle is selling for a record $50,087.
Redwood Materials is using computer vision and machine learning to identify and sort batteries by chemistry before they’re fed into the company’s rotary calciner — a massive cylindrical industrial furnace used to process 40,000 metric tons of raw feedstock a year.
Tesla said it will spend about $3.3 billion to expand its Berlin gigafactory to produce Cybercabs — yet another signal of the company’s global autonomy ambitions.
Over the weekend, Tesla invited “select customers” to preorder the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.” The Cybercab is priced at $29,990, but there is a lot more to ownership. The company will charge owners $299 a month to use the vehicles, delivery will only occur in a handful of cities, and operations will be limited to specific locations.
Uber opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities. Uber already has a service for teenagers. If this program proves successful, it would open Uber up to another market of customers: busy families.
Meanwhile, Uber said it’s notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in an October data breach.
Zipline continues to scale its autonomous drone delivery business, this time in its partnership with Uber. The companies had previously announced a partnership for drones to deliver for Uber Eats, but it officially launched this week in a Houston suburb. The aim is a big one: Uber and Zipline say they aim to make 1 million deliveries a day using the startup’s drones by the end of 2029.
One more thing …
I had a chance to catch up with (and interview) Ro Gupta, the head of Woven Capital — Toyota’s growth fund.
I’ve known Gupta for years; we first met when I worked at Fortune and he had a startup called Carmera. A lot has happened since those AV 1.0 days, and Gupta caught us up on this next era of AV innovation and where Toyota is interested in investing. It’s not enough to simply state “AI.” There’s more to it than that. Take a listen.

articles.title: Ukraine revives its grounded fleet of 500+ US-made Puma drones with homegrown anti-jamming tech — anti-jamming upgrade triples range to 31 miles
articles.text:
Ukraine revives its grounded fleet of 500+ US-made Puma drones with homegrown anti-jamming tech — anti-jamming upgrade triples range to 31 miles
The battlefield continues to evolve.
The U.S. delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions. These hand-launched uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are equipped with optical and infrared sensors for surveying the battlefield, but the evolving electromagnetic warfare landscape meant that the entire fleet had to be grounded. Now, Ukrainian defense firm Rise Technologies has upgraded the drones with its Palych communications system, which allows the UAVs to withstand the advanced electronic warfare (EW) environment found on the frontlines in 2026. According to United24 Media, this new component allows drone operators to select the drone’s operating frequency band to avoid heavily jammed channels and maintain communications during flight. It also increases the range of the Puma to 31 miles (50 kilometers) from its basic range of 10 miles (16 kilometers).
Russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations to counter the countermeasures, like the use of fiber optic drones, which are essentially jam-proof, and the installation of a camera and magnetic compass on Russian drones to counter GPS jamming. Ukraine has also devised a "flying modem" relay system for its drones, allowing its forces to conduct strategic drone strikes even without the use of finicky Starlink connections. The indigenous communications system was also installed on other drones from DJI and Autel, as well as on some attack UAVs, giving Ukrainian drone operators an advantage on the battlefield.
The proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them. The U.S. has already deployed high-energy lasers to shoot down Mexican cartel drones crossing its southern border, while the Royal Navy is testing the DragonFire laser that can target UAVs traveling at up to 400 mph while only costing $13 per shot. Israel has also deployed its 100,000-watt Iron Beam system, while China has built a man-portable anti-drone laser system that weighs 55 pounds and can hit targets up to 1,600 feet away.
These laser systems are ideal for taking down a few drone units. But for drone swarm threats, microwave systems are a better solution, as they could take down multiple drones in a single shot. Some examples of this include the Leonidas AGV from the U.S. and Turkey’s Aselsan Ejderha, or “Dragon” in English, which uses high-power electromagnetic systems to overwhelm the sensitive electronics found inside most drones.

articles.title: Notée 5/5, cette batterie externe UGreen passe sous les 50 € pendant le Black Friday 2026
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 : La batterie externe UGreen 25000 mAh Nexode Power Bank "5 étoiles" à 49,99 € (-23%)
Capabable d'alimenter jusqu'à trois appareils en même temps grâce à sa charge rapide, la batterie externe UGreen 25000 mAh Nexode Power Bank est actuellement notée 5/5 par notre rédaction. Pour le Black Friday 2026, son prix tombe à 49,99 € chez Amazon Marketplace, soit une baisse d'environ 23 % et 15,00 € d'économie.
UGreen propose avec la batterie externe 25000 mAh Nexode Power Bank un équipement pensé pour recharger rapidement des appareils lors de déplacements prolongés. Ce modèle associe une réserve importante d'énergie à un débit de charge élevé. L'appareil avait convaincu notre laboratoire lors de ses essais.
À l'occasion du Black Friday, la batterie descend à 49,99 € chez Amazon Marketplace, soit environ 23 % de moins que le prix moyen constaté ces 30 derniers jours (64,99 €). Cela représente une économie de 15,00 €.
Trois appareils alimentés en même temps et une charge rapide
Cette batterie externe UGreen affiche actuellement la note maximale de 5/5 sur notre site. Le boîtier permet d'alimenter jusqu'à trois appareils simultanément, ce qui évite d'avoir à choisir quel appareil brancher en priorité lors d'un déplacement. Pour suivre le niveau d'énergie restant sans incertitude, la façade intègre un écran de contrôle rapide indiquant l'état de la réserve.
L'appareil assure une charge rapide aussi bien en sortie vers vos terminaux qu'en entrée lors de sa propre recharge sur secteur, comme nous l'avons souligné dans notre test complet.
UGreen 25000 mAh Nexode Power Bank
Points forts
- Charge rapide (entrée et sortie).
- Écran de contrôle rapide.
- Possibilité de charger trois appareils simultanément.
Points faibles
- Capacité légèrement moindre qu'annoncé.
- Poids forcément élevé, haute capacité oblige.
NB : La baisse de prix rapportée est calculée en comparant le prix le plus bas du jour avec la moyenne des prix les plus bas pratiqués par tous les marchands pour le produit le mois dernier, avec des règles de sécurité pour écarter les prix des boutiques dont la politique en matière de TVA n’est pas claire (dites boutiques “grises”, typiquement en cas d’import de Chine).
Une réserve de 25000 mAh pensée pour les longues sorties
Avec une capacité nominale annoncée de 25000 mAh, cette référence s'adresse en priorité aux personnes qui s'éloignent longtemps d'une prise murale ou qui transportent plusieurs équipements électroniques au quotidien.
Notre examen a relevé une capacité réelle légèrement inférieure à celle annoncée par le fabricant ainsi qu'un poids élevé lié à cette grande réserve, deux caractéristiques qui ne poseront aucune difficulté si vous transportez la batterie dans un sac à dos plutôt que dans une poche de veste.
Xiaomi 67W Power Bank 10000 : l'autre option face au UGreen 25000 mAh Nexode Power Bank
La Xiaomi 67W Power Bank 10000 affiche elle aussi une note de 5/5 à ce jour sur notre site. Elle mise sur une approche plus compacte tout en intégrant directement un câble de charge, évitant ainsi le transport d'accessoires supplémentaires dans ses affaires. Son tarif est inférieur de 5,08 € à celui du modèle UGreen remisé.
Si la Xiaomi séduit par son câble intégré et son prix plus bas, la UGreen 25000 mAh Nexode Power Bank reste un choix plus pertinent pour les utilisateurs qui ont besoin d'alimenter trois appareils en même temps grâce à sa capacité de 25000 mAh.
Xiaomi 67W Power Bank 10000
Points forts
- Câble intégré jouant les dragonnes.
- Capacité réelle proche des chiffres annoncés.
- Charge rapide.
Points faibles

articles.title: Una jaguar recorre 2.100 kilómetros cruzando todo Brasil con un objetivo: preservar su especie
articles.text:
Jataí es una jaguar melánica con un pelaje predominantemente oscuro, característico del melanismo (coloquialmente, una pantera negra), pesa casi 90 kg y que nació hace aproximadamente cuatro años en el Refugio Biológico de Bela Vista, en Brasil, como cuenta el Correio Braziliense.
Igual que hay gente que se hace varias horas en autobús para quedar con su cita de Tinder, el pasado martes 10 de noviembre, Jataí emprendió un largo viaje de 2.100 kilómetros hasta el Cerrado brasileño, explica la corporación responsable de su refugio de nacimiento: allí tenía una cita para conservar su especie.
Hay match. Jataí salió del refugio gestionado por Itaipu, desde el oeste de Paraná, hasta la Reserva de Conservación Piracema, en el municipio de Almas, en Tocantins. Allí le esperaba un macho elegido por el Programa de Manejo de Poblaciones de Jaguares del Instituto Chico Mendes para la Conservación de la Biodiversidad con un objetivo: intentar tener crías, algo esencial para la supervivencia de este jaguar.
Por qué importa. El jaguar del bosque atlántico está en situación crítica: se estima que hay entre 25 y 53 jaguares adultos en el Corredor Verde de Argentina y Brasil, unas 7,5 veces menos que a principios de los 90. Y los pocos que quedan están dispersos y aislados en los fragmentos de bosque que quedan, lo que dificulta la diversidad genética.
No basta con reproducirse. De hecho, cuando la población es tan pequeña y está separada geográficamente como pasa con estos jaguares, aumenta la consanguinidad, se debilita la especie y aumenta el riesgo de extinción. De ahí que planifiquen los emparejamientos de los jaguares.
Rose Gasparini Morato, veterinaria del Centro Nacional de Investigación y Conservación de Mamíferos Carnívoros (Cenapi/ICMBio), cuenta que el programa tiene como objetivo formar las mejores parejas para que la población en cautiverio se convierta en una herramienta eficaz para la conservación de la especie en estado salvaje, funcionando como un grupo de seguridad. Jataí y su hermana Arapuá son hijas de Nena y Valente, una pareja fundadora, es decir, que fueron rescatados de la naturaleza, por lo que poseen una variabilidad genética esencial para el propósito de conservación de la especie.
Su nuevo hogar. El veterinario de Itaipú, Pedro Teles, detalla para Gaceta do Povo que "Si todo va bien, Jataí tendrá muchas crías y contribuirá a la preservación de este animal, tan importante para nuestro país y para el planeta". Creada en 2016 y con cinco mil hectáreas, la Reserva de Conservación Piracema es el primer centro de cría para la conservación reconocido legalmente en Tocantins y tiene programas de reproducción para especies nativas como tapires, osos hormigueros, pecaríes y pumas.
En esta fase de reproducción, la jaguar estará alojada en un recinto de más de 600 metros cuadrados, construido en medio de la vegetación natural del Cerrado y con agua fresca disponible de una cascada las 24 horas del día.
Un granito de arena. Aunque Jataí tenga crías que alivien la situación de conservación de la especie por el valor de su linaje, los problemas que abocaron al jaguar a la extinción siguen ahí, como la pérdida de su hábitat o la caza. Por otro lado, la reintroducción de animales criados en cautividad siempre supone un riesgo. En pocas palabras: la reproducción es solo el principio.

articles.title: Test de la Krups Coffee Crush Experience : compacte et élégante, mais un café assez basique — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le marché des machines à café avec broyeurs de grains est florissant. Notamment celui de l’entrée de gamme : des machines compactes et simples, destinées à des appartements urbains et des caféinateurs pressés. Face à Philips, DeLonghi ou Jura, Krups propose ses machines Coffee Crush, qui se distinguent de ses compétitrices par un format ultra compact et un design très épuré. La machine est ainsi la plus petite du marché. Mais que vaut le café qu’elle propose ? Qu’a-t-elle de plus à apporter que ses concurrentes ?
Voici notre retour d’expérience sur la toute dernière machine à café Krups, le modèle « Experience », le mieux équipé de la gamme Coffee Crush.
Fiche technique
| Caractéristique | Spécification | 
| Modèle / Référence | Krups Coffee Crush Experience (SA403BE0) | 
| Pression | 15 bars | 
| Puissance | 1150 – 1370 W | 
| Dimensions (L x l x H) | 29,5 x 15 x 36 cm | 
| Poids | 4 kg | 
| Capacité du réservoir d’eau | 1,8 L | 
| Mouture | 5 niveaux de réglage + trappe pour café moulu (décaféiné) | 
| Boissons proposées | Espresso, Lungo, Café Filtre, Cold Brew, Décaféiné, Boissons lactées, Eau chaude | 
| Durée de garantie | 2 ans | 
| Disponibilité des pièces détachées | 15 ans (engagement de réparabilité Krups) | 
La machine du test a été prêtée par la marque.
Design et ergonomie
Dès le déballage, il faut bien avouer que la machine fait son effet. La qualité des matériaux ainsi que celle de fabrication est à la hauteur. Les plastiques sont de qualité, Krups ayant judicieusement opté pour du mat qui ne prend pas les traces de doigts. C’est d’autant plus intelligent que le panneau de contrôle, invisible quand la machine est éteinte, est tactile et intégré dans ce plastique mat. Même à l’utilisation quotidienne, la surface ne garde aucune trace de doigt : chapeau.
À l’œil, le design est vraiment réussi : elle est à la fois mignonne et d’une sobriété appréciable.
Le format mini de la machine surprend, de même que son poids plume (4 kg) : elle est particulièrement simple à déplacer et pourra trouver sa place dans n’importe quelle cuisine, même les plus exiguës. C’est vraiment remarquable pour une machine à grain.
Ce format étroit et hyper pratique est d’autant plus réussi que Krups n’a pas rogné sur la taille du réservoir à eau et à grain. Celui dédié à l’eau est surprenamment grand pour une machine aussi petite : 1,8 L, ce qui est très confortable pour une ou deux personnes. Il est en outre bien pensé avec sa petite poignée et son couvercle amovible, qu’on aurait préféré non amovible, mais on ne peut pas tout avoir vu la présence de la poignée. Le réservoir à grain, sur le dessus, est aussi suffisamment vaste. Il intègre un réglage de la finesse de mouture, de 1 à 5, ce qui est sur le papier un excellent point pour jouer sur la puissance du café. Dans les faits, j’ai tenté différents niveaux de moutures et je n’ai pas vraiment senti la différence…
Le café est moulu, pesé et tassé automatiquement en fonction de la boisson demandée. Une fois le café fait, il faut tout de suite s’occuper d’un peu d’entretien : le marc de café doit être vidé après chaque café, en tirant sur la petite poignée chromée. Il suffit ensuite d’appuyer sur le bouton-poussoir pour faire tomber le café dans la poubelle, puis de passer un coup d’eau. Le fait de devoir nettoyer cela, plutôt que la présence d’un bac à marc, a été beaucoup reproché à la machine.
Personnellement, je trouve cela parfaitement logique vu la taille de la machine. Krups n’aurait tout simplement pas pu faire rentrer un bac. En outre, la manipulation est simple et rapide à réaliser, donc ce n’est pas gênant – pour moi.
Pour conclure, d’un point de vue de l’ergonomie et du confort d’utilisation, c’est un quasi sans faute pour la Coffee Crush.
Fonctionnalités et performances
Le panneau de contrôle est très joli. Il est aussi tactile, réactif, et très simple à comprendre et à prendre en main. Même pas besoin de sortir le mode d’emploi : les fonctionnalités, l’intensité et les tailles sont parfaitement indiquées et intuitives. Un vrai point fort face à d’autres machines qui doivent parfois se débrouiller avec seulement deux ou trois boutons et sur lesquelles il faut jouer de différentes combinaisons pour les réglages.
Différents pictogrammes rouges s’allumeront s’il est nécessaire de remplir le réservoir d’eau, de vider le marc de café, ou encore s’il est nécessaire de réaliser un détartrage.
Nous avons testé la version la plus chère des Coffee Crush, la « Experience », qui est celle qui propose le plus de types de boissons et de fonctions, cinq en tout : Expresso, Lungo, Café filtre, Cold brew, Eau chaude et Vapeur. Pour chaque boisson, on peut choisir entre trois tailles : S, M et L.
J’ai personnellement regretté que ces tailles ne soient pas réglables, et c’est pour moi un des plus gros défauts de la machine. Peut-être cela n’en serait pas un si le lungo L correspondait vraiment à un grand café : il fait couler 110 mL, ce qui sera donc votre taille de café maximale. J’ai parfois dû refaire couler un expresso en plus pour avoir le mug de café que je souhaitais. Il aurait suffi que les tailles de café soient plus diverses et éloignées entre elles, surtout que l’on a deux fonctions, Expresso et Lungo, ce qui donne au final six possibilités de format. C’est dommage et ça manque de flexibilité pour l’utilisateur. En revanche, si vous buvez plutôt des expressos ou des cafés moyens, cela ne vous posera aucun problème.
Sur la fonction café Espresso, voici les formats au choix :
- S : 30 mL
- M : 40 mL
- L : 50 mL
La fonction Lungo, quant à elle, fait des tasses de :
- S : 60 mL
- M : 80 mL
- L : 110 mL.
L’extraction du café est lente, ce qui est un bon point. En revanche, la machine ne dispose que d’une seule buse – impossible donc de faire deux expressos simultanément.
Le réglage de la température du café est une des fonctionnalités de la Coffee Crush. C’est bien, mais j’ai trouvé que même à la température la plus élevée (sur trois choix), le café n’est pas très chaud. C’est OK, mais ça pourrait être plus.
Les fonctions café
Quel résultat sur un expresso ? Eh bien ne vous attendez pas à un résultat professionnel comme dans un coffee shop. La crema s’avère peu dense et épaisse, plutôt claire, avec une tendance à faire des bulles. Globalement, la machine peine à faire des cafés « forts », même en réglant la mouture au plus fin et en mettant l’intensité au maximum, sur trois grains. Ne vous attendez pas à un effet coup de fouet genre ristretto italien. La machine produit un café léger, équilibré, qui évite l’amertume, mais qui peine à déployer les arômes. Résultat : un café, expresso comme lungo, plutôt générique. Pas mauvais ni exceptionnel, juste, générique.
La fonction Cold Brew permet d’obtenir directement un café froid. La machine tire alors du café lentement, et vous obtenez un café clair, type filtre, effectivement froid, même pas tiède. C’est pratique si vous voulez préparer une boisson froide à base de café telle qu’un latte froid ou un américano glacé.
La fonction Filter coffee reproduit, comme son nom l’indique, un café filtre. Dans les faits, on obtient une sorte de lungo très léger, simplement plus long. Je n’ai pas été particulièrement convaincue de l’utilité de cette option, mais elle a le mérite d’exister.
La buse vapeur
La buse vapeur, située à droite de la machine, dispose de deux réglages distincts via un petit switch, au choix pour réaliser une mousse de lait ou simplement réchauffer un liquide (donc du lait généralement). Pourtant de petite taille, elle s’avère efficace pour produire une mousse de lait.
Si le résultat est un peu plus aléatoire (car manuel) que sur la Philips Baristina Latte, avec une mousse de lait moins épaisse et dense, cela reste néanmoins honnête face à d’autres machines à percolateur. Il faut bien sûr le bon geste en tenant correctement le récipient (de préférence en inox) en biais, mais l’on peut tout à fait réaliser une mousse de lait chaud pour son cappuccino, même sans être un pro.
Bon point : la tête de la buse se dévisse pour faciliter le nettoyage.
La buse vapeur a une autre utilité : la fonction « eau chaude », qui marche parfaitement, le tout sans attente. L’eau sort directement de la buse, sans préchauffage, à une température suffisante pour se préparer une tisane. En revanche elle ne sera pas assez chaude si vous voulez du 90°C.
Bruit
La cafetière de Krups n’est pas la plus silencieuse, ni la plus bruyante. Lors de la confection d’un café, la machine produit tout un tas de bruits variés, le plus sonore étant bien sûr le broyage du grain, mesuré à 60 dB à 50 cm de la machine. Le bruit pourra être dérangeant si votre cuisine est trop proche de la chambre. En revanche, durant l’extraction du café elle est bien plus silencieuse, avec 45 dB mesurés.
Entretien et durabilité
En plus de devoir vider et rincer après chaque café le tiroir à marc, il est bon de réaliser de temps à autre un rinçage de la machine, par exemple si vous ne l’avez pas utilisée depuis un petit temps. Il suffit d’appuyer simultanément sur les boutons Grains et Espresso pour activer le mode rinçage. La machine vous le signifiera via un voyant « Rinse » si cela est nécessaire.
Comme toutes les machines à café, cette dernière demande d’être détartrée régulièrement. La machine affiche un voyant rouge (CALC) lorsqu’il est temps de s’en occuper. Il faut alors remplir le réservoir d’eau et y verser un sachet de détartrant Krups, puis de maintenir enfoncés les boutons Grains et Lungo simultanément pendant 3 secondes. N’oubliez pas de placer un récipient sous la buse café et la buse vapeur.
En outre, Krups, qui appartient au groupe SEB, promet une mise à disposition des pièces détachées durant 15 ans, ce qui est un excellent point de durabilité.
Prix et disponibilité
À son tarif officiel, la Coffee Crush Experience est vendue 349,99 euros. Sur ce modèle précis, il existe un seul coloris (Lionness), une sorte de gris-taupe discret.
La Coffee Crush Experience trône au sommet de la gamme. En dessous, on trouve deux modèles moins onéreux, avec moins de fonctions :
- Coffee Crush (coloris vert lichen ou ivoire, deux fonctions Café, pas de buse vapeur) à 299,99 euros
- Coffee Crush Extra (coloris noir ou marron chai, trois fonctions Café, pas de buse vapeur) à 329,99 euros.

articles.title: Can a TV be too large? An investigation | TechCrunch
articles.text:
For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.
The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows.
In short: They look way better.
They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024.
At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic.
However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache.
In short: Not great.
I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain.
“I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.”
Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?”
There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen.
Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having.
In considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a big screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car.
After a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison.
Initial physiological reactions aside, the size of the 65-inch screen (and whether your living space actually has room for it) is still something that needs to be considered carefully by potential buyers. I recently moved into a place with a slightly bigger living room, which has given me the flexibility to install a bigger device. At my old apartment, however, this size of TV would have definitely felt like it was devouring the space.
Another slight frustration is that the C4 does not come with any detailed installation instructions. The screen (which is so wide it’s difficult to move without another person there to help you) comes detached from its base, and the user is just sort of expected to figure out how to effectively move and put together the two pieces. A quick YouTube video is all that is necessary to understand this process, but you have to be careful when moving and assembling the pieces so as not to scratch or damage the screen.
Once the whole thing is set up and assembled, the OLED is a truly beautiful thing to behold. The customization that’s possible, including advanced brightness and color control — and things like “Filmmaker Mode” (which claims to adjust each movie’s color and frame rate settings to those intended by the director) — make the user experience really powerful.
To sum up: The evo C4 is a really spectacular piece of equipment that has a lot to offer the avid home entertainment viewer — although there may be a bit of a learning curve before it makes your cinema dreams come true.
